title: AI is driving a boom in modestly successful software projects
content:
If AI is so great, why aren’t we seeing an explosion of new, amazing software products? If anyone can turn their idea into working software with coding agents, where is all that software? People have been asking this question for years. As far as I can tell, the answer is that it’s spread out over a lot of modestly successful projects:

  • Somewhere between 2x and 20x new software is being created, depending on where you look
  • There’s no real growth in massively successful software projects (not counting AI tools)
  • There is around 2x growth in modestly successful software projects

Where all the new software is

I picked1 around twenty separate sources — software marketplaces, plugin registries, modding platforms, etc — which expose installation counts. I then compared the number2 of successful software projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26: i.e. before and after agentic coding hit the mainstream in mid-2025.

There’s a clear jump in modestly (not wildly) successful projects. For instance, the NVDA screen-reader addons directory had a bit over twice as many new addons with more than a thousand downloads (though no change in addons with more than ten thousand). The HACS open-source home automation community plugins store likewise saw twice as many new addons with over a hundred installs but no change in ones with over a thousand. New Steam games with over a hundred reviews are about 60% more common now than pre-2024. Obsidian plugins, Firefox and Chrome extensions, Nexus game mods, and Blender extensions had the same pattern. The Google Play store, WordPress plugins, and a few others didn’t show this pattern, but I think it’s still enough to conclude that AI is indeed driving a boom in hobbyist software.

Why addons and plugins?

I think examining addons, mods, and plugins is useful for a few reasons. First, it’s usually pretty easy to tell how many people are using them, or at least have installed them. Obviously AI is letting people produce a lot of software — I work at GitHub, so I see this first-hand, but the explosion in vibe-coded repos is clear to everyone — but without checking installation counts it’s unclear how much of this is actually being used.

Second, it’s a good way to minimize the amount of software that’s about AI. It doesn’t tell us much about AI’s effect on software to point out all the successful software projects that help people code with AI. That’s just selling shovels. The real question is whether AI is helping generate software that solves people’s ordinary problems.

AI-generated game mods and ports are a great example of this, because gamers aren’t trying to change the world with AI coding. They just want to play multiplayer Halo CE in the browser, or fly a plane in Helldivers, or play Super Smash online with rollback netcode. It’s looking like3 AI can supply this need effectively.

Were these projects actually AI generated?

Everyone is very coy about AI usage in hobbyist communities. In the rare cases where people admit it, they often get dogpiled. People really don’t like AI, even when it’s producing software they find useful. Given that, I don’t think it’s possible to use voluntary AI disclosure data to figure out whether AI is driving a software boom: the presence of the tag itself will discourage use, and many developers are just not going to admit it.

A 2x growth in successful projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26 is clearly something to do with AI, particularly in the background of a 10x growth in total projects. Of course not all of these projects will have AI involvement. But when people ask “why hasn’t AI improved software”, they’re talking about a missing trend4: wondering where all the new software is. As it turns out, it’s going towards a lot of small software projects that a few hundred or thousand people find useful.

Why small, moderately successful projects?

Why is AI growth visible in small projects but not big software companies? Why is it concentrated in moderately successful products and not wildly successful ones? I don’t have any data for this, but here’s my speculation.

Big, successful software companies often have all the visible features they want That’s why there’s not a wild explosion of new features in, say, macOS or Gmail: what would those features even be? As I’ve written about before, they’re also technically paralyzed by the features they have, so it’s not trivial for even very good coding agents to add new ones. Finally, many new features in successful products are subtle (e.g. enterprise compatibility things that almost all users will never encounter, or purely internal systems that slightly increase reliability).

It’s less clear to me why there aren’t many new wildly successful hobbyist projects. Maybe it’s just hard to have a really good idea for a product, and AI can’t help with that. Or maybe it takes years for a really successful project to develop, and we need to be patient for the current crop of thousand-user tools to grow into hundred-thousand-user tools.

  1. As you might expect, this research was all done with the help of AI. It wasn’t purely vibed — I gave a lot of feedback about where and how to look — but I would definitely not have scraped or analyzed this much data on my own. If you want to see the actual research data (or more likely point an agent at it), I’ve pushed it here.

    ↩

  2. Sometimes scaling to take into account platform growth. For instance, between the two windows I measured, Obsidian relaxed their requirement that all new plugins be reviewed by an admin, which predictably caused an explosion of plugins on the marketplace.

    ↩

  3. It certainly seems like it can so far, but who knows. Maybe once the hype has died down people will return to less buggy artisanal human-made mods and ports.

    ↩

  4. They might also be asking “why hasn’t the software I use gotten better?” For that, see my thoughts in the final section of this post.

    ↩

title: ★ Initial Thoughts on This Week’s New Apple TV 4K (4th Generation) and HomePod Mini 2
content:
Apple Newsroom, Tuesday morning:

The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing.

This is nice, but I don’t think it buys me anything, because my existing Apple TV 4K is paired with 2nd-gen HomePods, and the HomePods each have a “four-microphone design for far-field Siri”.

The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2× faster GPU performance than the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth.

The new AV1 decoder seems like it might be meaningful, but does anyone think UI navigation and animation smoothness is improved by going from the A15 to the A19 SoC? I mean navigation is going up/down/left/right. I’m sure the graphics and CPU improvements matter for gaming, but the only mention of gaming in Apple’s own Newsroom announcement is this sentence: “With Apple Fitness+, the living room becomes a workout studio, while Apple Arcade and the App Store’s library of games turn it into a home arcade.” I wish it were otherwise, but gaming is such an afterthought on Apple TV that it only garnered the second half of a sentence that started with Fitness+, a service that has only been in the news this year because Mark Gurman says Apple laid off part of the team.

The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on the remote — making it far easier to locate.

That’s my single favorite feature in the announcement. I hate to say it though, but the previous remote should have supported these features. The 3rd-gen Apple TV 4K came in 2022, but Apple launched AirTags with Precision Finding in 2021. Remote controls are right after keys on the list of things people misplace most frequently, and Apple’s remote controls, because they’re small and thin, are particularly susceptible to being snatched by couch-cushion gremlins. Speakers, so the remote can play a sound to help you find it, were invented even earlier than 2021.

Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as the front and rear speaker pairs match.

This is tempting to try. In other words, in addition to the two 2nd-gen HomePods I already have paired in my living room, I can add two of the new HomePod Mini 2’s behind the sofa for surround sound.

The elephant in the room, though, is price. Before this week, Apple sold two models of the 3rd-generation Apple TV. On a percentage basis, they were hit the hardest of any products Apple sells by the company’s across-the-board price increases this summer:

BeforeJune 25Change
HomePod$300$35017%
(Old) HomePod Mini$100$13030%
(Old) Apple TV 64 GB$130$20054%
(Old) Apple TV 128 GB$150$25067%

The new Apple TV 4K announced this week only comes in one model, and it costs $300. It’s great that there’s only one model for simplicity’s sake, but the number one complaint when the previous generation cost $130/150 was that it was too expensive compared to set-top boxes and sticks from Amazon and Roku. (Or the “free” option of using the “smart TV” software that comes with every TV set.) Now, with the new Apple TV, it’s twice as expensive — and Apple is not keeping the 3rd-gen models around as lower-priced options. I still think it’s worth it, personally, but the general consumer market thought the old prices were too high and I don’t see any of the new features making Joe or Jane Consumer think “Sure, I was skeptical about the old one at $130, but this new model, which looks exactly the same, this seems worth $300.”

HomePod Mini 2 now costs $150. That’s not too much of an increase over the new-since-June-25 $130 price for the old HomePod Mini, but it’s a stiff 50 percent increase from the old HomePod Mini’s $100 price from November 2020 through June 24 this year. I generally round Apple’s prices up from their “99” values, but it’s worth noting that what I’m calling $100 was actually $99, and going to just two digits does have a psychological effect on buying behavior. Again, I think $150 is a reasonable price for the HomePod Mini 2, but it doesn’t feel as much like a lark as $99 did. $99 was a bit of a “Sure, let’s get another one” price; $150 is more of a “Do we really need another one of these?” price.

At the old pre-June prices, you could buy a 128 GB Apple TV and a pair of HomePod Minis for $350 ($150 + $100 + $100). Four short months later, with today’s new models, that combination would cost $600 ($300 + $150 + $150). That price difference is much more striking than any of the new and improved features in the products.

title: This video is 2 minutes long
content:
As I mentioned before, it takes me way too long to edit a single video. So I am releasing it in chunks. If I never finish it, well then at least I'll have a few videos out.

What is the video about? Well, it is about the future we were promised, versus the one we are actually living in. It's not dystopian, but it seems like the goal of tech is supposedly to automate the tedious and mundane, so we can have more time to do the things we love. But along the way came the word productivity. The goal of productivity is not to get free time. It is to produce more in the same amount of time. Not produce more in less time. Read this a couple times for it to stick.

Click the image to load

The first one was 1 minute long. Today's will be two minutes. And the next will be 3 minutes long. Then I'll have to think about Fibonacci.

Load-bearing (permalink)

You find the weirdest stuff inside your walls. Our house was built in 1949 and we're its third owner, and I have no idea what those other people were doing, but at one point someone installed a junction box full of live, bare wires that they filled with crumpled newspaper (!); and don't get me started on the decision not to put vapor barriers in the kitchen windows (we were one good shake away from the entire front of the house falling down when we discovered that one, and while it cost us an extra $19,000 to fix, that was still cheaper than rebuilding the whole front of the house).

Plus there was the unpermitted drainage system installed down the side of the house that must have attracted some (undocumented) planning inspector negativity; at least, that's the only reason I can think of for someone to have filled those drains with concrete (!!), a fact we discovered during the first heavy rainfall after moving in, when the water rose to shin-height (!!!).

But the weirdest and most nerve-wracking mysteries were the "structural" members of dubious quality, placement and utility. Some of them only seemed to be holding stuff up, but on closer inspection turned out to be free-floating 2x4s, not anchored to anything. On more than one occasion, our builders have moved jacks into position and removed those random uprights, only to discover that they weren't holding anything up.

Say what you will about this method, but it is decisive: if you remove a vertical member and nothing falls down, you can be pretty sure that wasn't a load-bearing member.

(This is a metaphor about AI.)

You can be forgiven for rolling your eyes when the subject of "digital sovereignty" comes up. Rhetorically, "digital sovereignty" is a coded way for a politician to say, "We should build a fuckton of AI data-centers while bypassing any environmental review":

https://datacentremagazine.com/technology-and-ai/keir-starmers-2bn-pledge-how-the-uk-plans-to-advance-ai

But AI has nothing to do with digital sovereignty. It is not load-bearing. All it takes to understand this is a little thought-experiment. Imagine that we removed all the chatbots from Canada, or the UK, or the EU, or the USA. What would fall down?

Nothing important.

Every public administrative body – national, regional and local – would continue to function. Every firm – large and small – would continue to trade. Households would be unscathed, save for their youngest members, who would suffer the indignity and tedium of having to do their own homework again.

Which is not to say that "digital sovereignty" is a nothingburger. The walls of our nations are filled with load-bearing digital members. It's just that these are the most boring, regular-degular-ass technologies imaginable.

Like Microsoft Office 365. Take away M365 and every ministry collapses, every firm shutters, and many if not most households will be in serious trouble.

And here's the thing: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella paid $1m out of his own pocket to join the murderer's row of tech CEOs who sat behind Trump on the inaugural dais:

https://apnews.com/article/trump-inauguration-tech-billionaires-zuckerberg-musk-wealth-0896bfc3f50d941d62cebc3074267ecd

Microsoft donated $10 million to Trump's Epstein Memorial Ballroom:

https://www.geekwire.com/2026/leaked-list-shows-what-microsoft-amazon-and-other-tech-giants-are-giving-for-the-white-house-ballroom/

Microsoft provides the back-end administrative infrastructure for Trump's racist pogroms (take away M365 and ICE would collapse):

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/feb/17/ice-microsoft-technology-immigration-crackdown

The CEO of Microsoft France admitted that if Trump ordered the company to spy on French citizens' data (or the data of the French government), his company would comply, in secret:

https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/

And here's the kicker: Microsoft has terminated the M365 and Outlook access of international public officials whose official acts made Trump angry, starting with the Chief Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, who lost his accounts after he swore out the genocide warrant for Netanyahu:

https://www.computerweekly.com/opinion/Microsofts-ICC-email-block-reignites-European-data-sovereignty-concerns

This is a white-hot, 278-alarm digital sovereignty dumpster-fire. M365 – as well as cloud software from Oracle, Google, Apple, Amazon and other US tech giants that have fused themselves with the Trump regime in exchange for tax breaks and antitrust forbearance – is load-bearing, and worse, those 2x4s are filled with termites and dry-rot.

Digital sovereignty is as real as real can be. It just has nothing to do with AI. AI isn't load-bearing. Boring-ass tech monopolist cloud software is…and we can not trust it:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

title: Book Review: Africa Is Not A Country - Breaking Stereotypes of Modern Africa by Dipo Faloyin ★★★★⯪
content:
It's hard to craft a book with so much righteous indignation - let alone make it funny, accessible, and informative. Nevertheless, Dipo Faloyin has succeeded in writing a spectacular takedown of the myths which are often perpetrated about Africa.

It starts in the best way possible:

[Insert generic African proverb here. Ideally an allegory about a wise monkey and his interaction with a tree, or the relationship between the donkey and the ant that surprisingly speaks to grand gestures of valour. Sign it off: Ancient African proverb]

How many times have you seen that? Think about all the tropes played out in every Hollywood movie set vaguely in Africa - would you accept the same stereotypes about your continent?

And yet, it does rely a little too much about internalised stereotypes:

The point is: there are a lot of people in Lagos. None of them are shy.

I'm sure there's at least one introvert in Lagos who cringes every time people expect them to be boisterous!

The horrors and complexities of colonisation and its aftermath are on display for all to see. In many way, much like cryptobros discovering why banking regulations exist, some African countries are speed-running Europe's history of bloody internecine warfare and mad kings. A predilection that some parts of Europe (and America) are still struggling to move past.

I think it could have benefited from just a few maps or illustrations. I also found some of the language a little… infantilising? The way he capitalises certain phrases like "These Powerful Men In The Capital" felt to me a little out of place. That said, there's some excellent caustic humour and some quite beautiful prose.

In the end, it shows that while Africa is not a country, the stories are often of different countries tackling the same problems in the same ways. [Insert something about everyone's hearts beating to the rhythm of an African drum, while an elephant wanders into an impossibly huge sunset.]
